feedback: If a learner says it is dark because the deep is far from the sky or space, redirect to the water itself absorbing and scattering the light as it passes through.
If a learner says the whole ocean is dark, anchor the surface as bright and sunlit (where swimmers and snorkellers can see) and trace darkness increasing with depth.
activities.intendedInsight: The deep ocean is dark because water absorbs and scatters sunlight as it travels down, so 'why does it get dark?' is grounded in how light behaves, not just asserted.
learnerActions: Recall prior learning that light travels and that we see things because light enters our eyes.
Investigate or observe light shining through more and more water, using slightly tinted or milky water as a model of many metres of seawater, and describe how it dims.
Explain, in their own words, why it gets dark deep down — because water absorbs and scatters light with depth, not because the deep is 'far from the sky or space'.
State that light fades gradually with depth rather than switching off suddenly.
activities.title: Connect to how light behaves in water

feedback: If a learner picks the deep bottom because it has the most space, redirect from space to food: plants need light, and animals go where the food is, and light (so food) is greatest at the top.
If a learner says sunlight reaches all the way to the seabed, show light dimming to nothing with depth and re-name the zones by how much light reaches them.

Correct answer to the 'most room' claim: most ocean life lives near the top in the sunlight zone, not the deep bottom. Deeper down, sunlight fades through the dim twilight zone to the totally dark midnight zone. Phytoplankton need light to grow and make food, and they are the base of the food chain, so most animals gather near the surface where there is light and food.
For the seaweed question: seaweed (a kind of algae) needs light to make food, just like plants do, so it cannot grow on the deep dark seabed where no sunlight reaches.
activities.intendedInsight: Most ocean life lives near the surface because plants need light to make food and form the base of the food chain; light fades through twilight to a dark midnight zone — yet some life still survives deeper by other means.
learnerActions: Put the three zones in order by depth, top to bottom.
Answer: what happens to light as you go deeper? (It fades until it is gone.)
Answer and explain: which zone has the most life, and why? (The sunlight zone — plants need light to make food.)
Respond to a claim such as 'The deep bottom must be where MOST sea life lives — there's the most room down there' by saying whether it is right and explaining why.
Consider a counterexample: a deep-sea anglerfish does live in the midnight zone with no sunlight — discuss how life can still exist deep, but differently, even though most life is near the surface.
Answer: could a seaweed grow on the deep dark seabed? Why or why not?
activities.title: Explain and check the light–life connection
